title: Paloma and the Bridge
premise: In the river city of Vessengard, 1911, apprentice clockmaker Jonah Yarrow is summoned to the observatory to repair its failing master clock, a job meant to keep them safely unremarkable. Instead, they find a child—Liesl, daughter of executed revolutionary Anselm Voss—left at the door with orders to forget her face. Jonah, who once promised Voss in peacetime that his family would never stand alone, must hide Liesel among the clockmakers' quarter while the state hunts her and Jonah's own master weighs betrayal against conscience. As the river ice groans toward spring, Jonah smuggles Liesel across the bridge on the night of the thaw, paying for it with their invisibility, their apprenticeship, and nearly their life—but keeping the promise intact, and finding that the found family they built was worth every cost.
about_author: Ulyana Amberdale is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing the confiscated letters of political prisoners before turning to fiction. She writes from a drafty house near a decommissioned observatory, where she keeps three clocks running slightly out of sync on purpose.

chapters.title: The Clock That Lost Its Heart
chapters.summary: Jonah Yarrow, POV. Summoned to the observatory to repair the master clock whose escapement has failed, Jonah takes quiet pride in being invisible—history happens elsewhere. Inside, they find the mechanism sabotaged deliberately, and a note: 'Fix it, and wait.' The beat is unease beneath routine competence.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At dawn, a girl of eight, Liesl, is left at the observatory door with coins and an instruction: forget this face. Jonah recognizes her father's surname—Anselm Voss, the revolutionary just declared enemy of the state. The emotional beat is terror colliding with an old, half-forgotten promise.

chapters.title: What Was Promised in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Alternating Jonah and flashback POV. A memory surfaces: years earlier, a young Voss repaired Jonah's mother's clock without charge, and Jonah swore his family would never stand alone. Now Voss is dead and his daughter sleeps in the clock room. The beat is the weight of words spoken when they cost nothing.

chapters.title: The Master's Silence
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Master Horvath notices the extra ration of bread, the small shoes by the door—and says nothing, which is worse than anger. Meanwhile, inspectors question the observatory staff about the sabotage. The beat is dread: silence can be loyalty or a debt being saved up.

chapters.title: Lessons in Small Hours
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, with Liesl's voice emerging. Hiding Liesel among the clocks, Jonah teaches her gears and patience; she teaches Jonah what fear looks like worn lightly. The found family forms around brass and lamplight. The beat is tenderness sharpened by the knowledge it cannot last.

chapters.title: The Informer's Ledger
chapters.summary: Inspector Brandt's POV. Brandt, ambitious and not cruel, closes in: the sabotage points to sympathizers in the clockmakers' quarter, and a child matching Liesl's description survived. He offers Horvath immunity for names. The beat is corruption as bureaucracy—power corrupting through paperwork, not violence.

chapters.title: Horvath's Choice
chapters.summary: Horvath's POV. The old master, once imprisoned under a previous regime, must choose: give up the girl and keep his craft alive, or burn his life's work protecting a stranger's child. He chooses, quietly, to forge a travel permit using his guild seal. The beat is an old man reclaiming his conscience.

chapters.title: Ice Breaking on the River
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The thaw begins early; the bridge will be watched at first light when the ice breaks and traffic surges. Brandt returns with a warrant. Jonah, Liesel, and Horvath have one night to prepare papers, disguises, and a route. The beat is breathless resolve—the point of no return.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, climax. Amid the spring crowds and cracking ice, Jonah walks Liesel across the bridge while Brandt closes in; Horvath creates a diversion at the tollhouse and is seized. Jonah hands Liesel to Voss's old comrades on the far bank, keeping the promise at last. The beat is sacrifice and triumph entangled.

chapters.title: The Face Worth Remembering
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, resolution. Months later, Jonah works openly now—arrested briefly, released, no longer invisible but no longer safe either, and freer for it. A letter arrives from Liesel, signed with a drawing of a clock. The master clock runs true again. The beat is quiet justice outside the law, and belonging earned.
